item.title: CIS 115 - Introduction to Computing Science
item.description: Course Description A survey of the discipline of Computing Science and its interaction with other disciplines, incorporating historical development, theories, and tools of Computing Science (algorithm design and programming). Topics include: mechanical and digital computers, computational thinking, security, simulation, data science, web technologies, and more. Students will be able to explore real-world problems within computer science and research current topics. Credit Hours 2 credits Course Overview This course is an introduction to the history, fundamental theories, basic programming, and research areas within Computing Science and its related disciplines. Computing Science has a direct impact on many facets of daily life, but very few of us ever take the time to wonder how it all works. This course aims to fill that void.

item.title: CIS 116 - Introduction to Programming
item.description: Course Description An introduction to programming by exploring core concepts such as variables, conditionals, iteration, basic data structures, functions, and classes. Hands-on activities to learn and apply concepts to real-world problems and ideas. Students will gain a solid foundation in programming, setting the stage for further study and professional use. Credit Hours 1 credit Course Overview This course serves as a primary introduction to modern programming by exploring core concepts such as variables, conditionals, iteration, and functions. To accomplish this goal, we will do several hands-on learning activities. While doing so, we will try to relate the concepts we are learning to real-world problems and ideas. Students will gain a solid foundation in programming, setting the stage for further study and professional use.

item.title: CIS 118 - International Professional Development Experience
item.description: Course Description Participation in various professional development activities at an international university. Credit Hours 1 credit Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD Course Prerequisites TBD

item.title: CIS 120 – Web Foundations
item.description: Course Description The Internet, web browsers, and web-page-development technology: web-page design and implementation with Hypertext Markup Language (HTML), CSS, and JavaScript utilizing a modern webpage design. Students will also get hands-on experience deploying their own website. Course Overview This course. Course Goals and Learning Outcomes Construct standards-compliant web pages using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript while maintaining separation of concerns. Develop accessible web pages that conform to established usability and accessibility guidelines. Implement responsive, modern page layouts and visual styling using CSS. Create interactive web functionality through JavaScript and Document Object Model manipulation. Retrieve, process, and display data from Web APIs using JavaScript. Evaluate websites using industry standards for user experience and design quality. Course Prerequisites None.

item.title: CIS 140 – Foundations of Artificial Intelligence
item.description: Course Description Hands-on introduction to Artificial Intelligence (AI). This course explores foundational topics like data handling, supervised and unsupervised learning, neural networks, natural language processing, computer vision, and the ethical implications of AI. Interactive labs and projects are used to develop real AI applications and reflect on their impact in society. Course Overview This course. Course Goals and Learning Outcomes Describe the fundamental concepts of artificial intelligence and data science and their roles in modern society. Identify common applications of AI and data science across a variety of disciplines and industries. Explain the basic data science workflow, including data collection, preparation, analysis, and interpretation. Use introductory data analysis tools to explore and visualize datasets. Interpret and communicate insights derived from data analyses and AI-generated outputs. Recognize ethical, legal, and societal considerations associated with AI and data-driven decision making. Apply generative AI tools responsibly to support problem-solving, information analysis, and content creation. Evaluate the strengths and limitations of AI systems and data-driven models. Course Prerequisites Co or prerequisite CIS 116 (or equivalent programming course).

item.title: CIS 190 - Undergraduate Seminar in Computing and Information Science
item.description: Course Description Topics of special interest in computing and information sciences. Credit Hours 1–3 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD Course Prerequisites TBD

item.title: CIS 200 - Programming Fundamentals
item.description: Course Description Principles of algorithm design and their application to procedural programming: state, control structures, methods. Patterns of conditional and iterative control structure. Program testing. Introduction to arrays, classes, and objects. Programming projects. Credit Hours 4 credits Course Overview Learn the fundamentals of writing computer programs – specific instructions in a language that the computer can understand. Every computer application you use and every interactive website you visit is the result of a computer program. In this class, we will learn to write computer programs in Java and C# – however, the skills we will develop will apply to all programming languages.

item.title: CIS 209 - Computer Programming for Engineers
item.description: Course Description Application of computers to engineering problems. Abstraction and problem solving; algorithms; control structures; input/output; functions; arrays and array processing. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD Course Prerequisites TBD

item.title: CIS 225 - Foundations of Computer Networks
item.description: Course Description Survey of computer networking fundamentals, including 7-layer OSI model, common networking protocols, socket-based network programming, network security and encryption, and network performance and reliability basics. Credit Hours 1 credit Course Overview This course will introduce students to the core concepts of network communication between computing systems. Students will learn about the 7-layer OSI network model and how common networking protocols such as TCP/IP, HTTP, DHCP, DNS, and more work to form the foundation of the modern internet. Students will explore basic socket-based network programming, discuss security and encryption of network communications, and explore concepts related to network performance and reliability.

item.title: CIS 251 - Foundations of Cybersecurity
item.description: Course Description This course introduces the fundamental concepts of cybersecurity, including how digital systems communicate, common cyber threats, security principles, risk management, ethical considerations, and career opportunities in the field. Students will develop a cybersecurity mindset through case studies, discussions, and hands-on activities. Credit Hours 1 credit Course Overview This course serves as a basic introduction to cybersecurity with a focus on exploring common threats and mitigations. Students will learn key principles such as the CIA triad, authentication, authorization, encryption, trust, and more. The course will include case studies of common cybersecurity threats and incidents and discussions on how to prevent them in the future. Students should leave the course with a defensive mindset and an understanding of risks and vulnerabilities present in modern technology.

item.title: CIS 260 - Foundations of Relational Databases
item.description: Course Description This 1‑credit hour course introduces students to Structured Query Language (SQL) for retrieving and analyzing data in relational databases. Students will learn to write basic queries to select, filter, summarize, and combine data from multiple tables using hands‑on exercises and real‑world examples. Credit Hours 1 credit Course Overview The objective of this course is to provide students with the foundations to understand simple relational databases. With this knowledge, students will be able to understand and write SQL queries to find, organize, and summarize information from real-world datasets.

item.title: CIS 300 - Data and Program Structures
item.description: Course Description A study of common data and program structures together with associated algorithms. Topics include interfaces, design patterns, arrays, stacks, queues, lists, trees, hash tables, recursion, binary search, and tree traversals. Experience with both use and implementation of these structures and algorithms using a modern programming language. Discussion of tradeoffs involving performance and software maintainability. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Overview This course examines the fundamental data structures, algorithms, and software design principles used in modern computing. Students will learn to analyze, implement, and apply common data structures such as arrays, stacks, queues, lists, trees, graphs, hash tables and more, along with the algorithms that operate on them. Through hands-on programming experiences, students will explore interfaces, abstraction, and design patterns while developing solutions to computational problems and data structures. Emphasis is placed on evaluating algorithm efficiency, understanding performance tradeoffs, and selecting appropriate data structures to create efficient and maintainable software.

item.title: CIS 301 - Logical Foundations of Programming
item.description: Course Description Logical formalisms used to model and reason about computer systems. Propositional and predicate logic, syntax, semantics, and proof theory; soundness and completeness issues. Mathematical induction. Program verification: invariants and program logics. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Overview This course provides an introduction to formal logic and its application to mathematical reasoning and software correctness. Students will learn to represent and analyze logical statements using propositional and predicate logic, evaluate arguments and proofs, and apply formal reasoning techniques such as equivalence laws, deduction rules, contradiction, and induction. Topics include truth tables, sets, quantifiers, logical proofs, and the translation of natural language into formal symbolic expressions. The course also examines the use of logic in computing, with an emphasis on reasoning about program correctness through specifications, preconditions, postconditions, invariants, loops, functions, and program termination. By the end of the course, students will be able to apply formal methods to analyze logical arguments and verify the correctness of computational systems.

item.title: CIS 308 - C Language Laboratory
item.description: Course Description Fundamentals of programming in C. Credit Hours 1 credit Course Overview Not yet drafted — pending course-designer’s detailed pass. resources/reference/degree-maps/cs.md notes this course “might be replaced with any 1-credit programming language course” — not yet decided whether C specifically remains the vehicle under the redesign. Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD Course Prerequisites Prerequisite: CIS 300 (current catalog).

item.title: CIS 351 - Cyber Defense Basics
item.description: Course Description Knowledge and skills needed to administer and defend computer networks and systems. Topics include the basics of computer networks, intelligence gathering, network scanning and sniffing, password security and cracking, vulnerability exploitation, distributed denial of service, logging and auditing, and wireless network security and cracking. Practice using an isolated computing network. Credit Hours 1 credit Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD Course Prerequisites TBD

item.title: CIS 397 - Honors Seminar in Computer Science
item.description: Course Description Honors Seminar in Computer Science Credit Hours 1–3 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD Course Prerequisites TBD

item.title: CIS 400 - Object-Oriented Design, Implementation, and Testing
item.description: CIS 400 is being reimagined as a mid-level capstone course, where students use what they have learned in the first two years to create a significant programming project. This is not dissimilar to what the course currently does, but the current model utilizes highly prescriptive milestones that are trivialized by generative AI usage. Course Description A study of concepts and techniques used to produce quality software programs. Object-oriented concepts, models, execution environments, design and testing techniques. Extensive application of these concepts and techniques to the development of non-trivial software programs.

item.title: CIS 401 - Software Design, Implementation, and Testing
item.description: Course Description A study of concepts and techniques used to produce quality software programs. Software design concepts, models, execution environments, design and testing techniques. Extensive application of these concepts and techniques to the development of non-trivial software programs. The course culminates with a capstone project to demonstrate core understanding. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Overview This course is focused on helping you to learn the concepts and skills needed to develop high-quality software. Along the way you will have ample opportunities to practice these skills developing non-trivial software projects. These are not the “baby programs” of early CS coursework, but rather applications that could be used in a production environment.

item.title: CIS 415 - Ethics and Conduct for Computing Professionals
item.description: Course Description A study of the ethical issues raised by computing technologies and the impact on society. Exploration of how one might justify actions in regard to ethical dilemmas within the fields of technology, computer science, information security, and artificial intelligence. Other topics include an examination of terminology used, Profession Codes of Conduct for computer science professionals, ethics of software development, and ethical issues relating to privacy and intellectual property in cyberspace.

item.title: CIS 450 - Computer Architecture and Operations
item.description: Course Description Introduction to modern computer architectures: register transfer abstraction, addressing modes, basic operations (data transfer, arithmetic/logic, and control operations). Basic Operating System concepts and operations. Understanding relationships of higher-level language constructs to corresponding assembly instruction sequences generated by compilers. Introduction to interrupts and low-level I/O operations. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD Course Prerequisites Prerequisite: ECE 241 and CIS 308 (current catalog).

item.title: CIS 490 - Special Topics in Computer Science
item.description: Course Description Current topics in computer science. Credit Hours 1–4 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD Course Prerequisites TBD

item.title: CIS 497 - Undergraduate Research Experience
item.description: Course Description Open to students pursuing undergraduate research projects. Credit Hours 0–3 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD Course Prerequisites TBD

item.title: CIS 499 - Honors Research/Thesis
item.description: Course Description Individual research problem selected with approval of faculty advisor. A report/thesis is presented orally and in writing during the last semester. Credit Hours 2–4 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD Course Prerequisites TBD

item.title: CIS 501 - Software Architecture and Design
item.description: Course Description Principles and patterns for design and structure of software, development of object-oriented models, examples of software architecture. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD Course Prerequisites Prerequisite: CIS 400 (current catalog).

item.title: CIS 505 - Introduction to Programming Languages
item.description: Course Description History, programming language concepts including type, scope and extent, abstraction mechanisms and control; programming paradigms, including one or more of logic, functional, and object-oriented programming, and programming languages supporting the selected paradigms; interpreters, compilers and virtual machines for the selected languages; storage management and garbage collection; type checking and type inference. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD Course Prerequisites Prerequisite: CIS 301, CIS 400 (current catalog).

item.title: CIS 511 - Introduction to Agentic Software Engineering
item.description: Course Description This course introduces students to agentic software engineering: building software and systems with AI agents through disciplined, repeatable, and scalable practices rather than “vibe coding.” Credit Hours 3 credits Course Prerequisites Prerequisite: CIS 501 Course Overview The course begins by teaching students to implement a simple coding agent. LLM-based agents are themselves a computing platform: they operate through a set of primitives that includes calling an LLM with context, invoking tools, and receiving instructions from a human developer. Each step incurs costs and may introduce errors or security risks. To use agents effectively, students need to understand their anatomy, develop a mental model of their execution, estimate costs, and identify potential sources of failure and security vulnerabilities. This understanding also enables students to customize and extend agents for greater effectiveness and efficiency in a particular development context. The course also examines how agents interact with conventional development tools, such as testing frameworks and source code repositories, and how agentic development changes established practices or calls for new tools.

item.title: CIS 520 - Operating Systems I
item.description: Course Description Operating systems concepts, services, and implementation: interrupt processing, processes, concurrency, deadlocks, resource scheduling and system structure; resource management: real and virtual storage, input/output systems, disk scheduling and file systems; design and construction of concurrent programs. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD Course Prerequisites Prerequisite: CIS 450 or ECE 431; CIS 308, and CIS 400 or CIS 501 (current catalog).

item.title: CIS 522 - Introduction to Data Structures
item.description: Course Description Introduction to basic data structures such as stacks, queues, lists, and priority queues, and algorithmic techniques for sorting, searching and hashing. Emphasis on modularity and reuse. Introduction to the concept of object-oriented design and interface specifications. Credit Hours 1 credit Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD Course Prerequisites TBD

item.title: CIS 523 - Introduction to Concurrent Programming
item.description: Course Description Introduction to concurrent programming techniques based on message passing primitives (send/receive) and shared memory (semaphore based P/V operations and monitor-based wait/signal operations). Credit Hours 1 credit Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD Course Prerequisites TBD

item.title: CIS 525 - Introduction to Network Programming
item.description: Course Description Basic inter-process communication and network programming concepts including client-server and peer-to-peer, communication protocol use and specification, reliable and secure communication, and network applications including web technologies, electronic mail, and file transfer with a focus on application and implementation. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Overview Not yet drafted — pending course-designer’s detailed pass. resources/reference/degree-maps/cs.md lists this as one of three choices (with CIS 520, CIS 625) for the Year 4 Systems Elective, which “fulfils ABET networking and OS requirements; may become a regular tech elective instead.”

item.title: CIS 526 - Web Application Development
item.description: Course Description Fundamental principles and best practices of web development, user interface design, web API design, advanced web interfaces, web development frameworks, single-page web applications, web standards and accessibility issues. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD Course Prerequisites TBD

item.title: CIS 527 - Enterprise Systems Administration
item.description: Course Description Administration of the Linux operating system, including installation, configuration, distributed file systems, firewalls and security, shell scripting, and user account management. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes Upon completion of this course, students will be able to: Understand the major components of an enterprise level computer network and server system. Design and implement a simple enterprise level server system and network, as well as provision workstations on that network quickly and easily. Communicate information about enterprise systems clearly and effectively to users of all skill levels and interests. Develop ways to increase efficiency by automating tasks whenever possible using scripting and configuration management tools. Understand and describe security risks in any enterprise system and any ways that they can be mitigated. Show how to monitor enterprise systems for problems and use that information to locate and fix any issues within the system. Work with cloud technologies and describe how they can be integrated into an enterprise information technology setup. Course Prerequisites TBD

item.title: CIS 530 - Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
item.description: Course Description Fundamental background in intelligent systems for undergraduate students. Intelligent agents, problem-solving, uninformed and informed (heuristic) search, game tree search, foundations of knowledge representation and reasoning using logic and probability, and a first introduction to planning and machine learning. AI topics include the problem areas of natural language processing (NLP) and perception and methodologies such as artificial neural networks and genetic and evolutionary computation. Applications to practical design and development of intelligent systems will be emphasized, leading to individual projects on current topics and applications in AI.

item.title: CIS 531 - Introduction to Programming Techniques for Data Science and Analytics
item.description: Course Description Introduction to programming techniques for working with big data. Survey of programming concepts that underlie the MapReduce architecture, their implementation, and specific tools for data integration and data transformation. Basic databases and query processing in the context of real-world problems. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD Course Prerequisites TBD

item.title: CIS 532 - Introduction to Deep Learning
item.description: Course Description Foundations of deep learning, with focus on different types of modern neural network architectures (such as convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and transformers). Regularization and optimization in the context of deep learning. Frameworks and tools for building and training deep neural networks. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD Course Prerequisites TBD

item.title: CIS 533 - Introduction to Data Science Foundations
item.description: Course Description Introduction to the foundations of data science and data analytics. Computer science concepts used for making discoveries in data. Data wrangling, feature engineering, classification, regression, clustering, outlier detection, societal aspects of data science, and more. Analysis of real-word data. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes Upon completion of this course, students will be able to: Define and profile data science problems, and solve it using machine learning and data analytics tools. Understand and be able to apply basic machine learning and data analytic techniques. Identify machine learning and computing strategies to approach and solve problems using data. Understand discovery methods and their application to turn data into knowledge. Use statistical inference to explore data and determine the significance of discoveries. Course Prerequisites TBD

item.title: CIS 536 - Introduction to Computer Graphics
item.description: Course Description Introduction to computer graphics for undergraduate students. Mathematical foundations (e.g., linear, affine, and projective transformations) and fundamental topics in realistic rendering: view normalization, clipping and culling, scan conversion of lines and polygons, shading and illumination, texture mapping, user interfaces, picking, and collision handling. Intermediate topics include shaders, procedural textures, particle systems, basics of animation, fractals, color theory, and ray tracing. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD

item.title: CIS 537 - Computer Vision
item.description: Course Description Theory and applications of computer vision. Introduction to computer vision, introduction to image formation, Credit Hours 3 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD Course Prerequisites TBD

item.title: CIS 551 - Fundamentals of Computer and Information Security
item.description: Course Description An introduction to computer and information security, including common attack techniques, application of cryptography in security, authentication and authorization, network security, enterprise network defense, web security, and analysis of design flaws that render a system vulnerable. Course projects provide hands-on experience on both the defense and offense aspects in cyberspace. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD Course Prerequisites TBD

item.title: CIS 553 - Fundamentals of Cryptography
item.description: Course Description Introduction to the fundamentals of cryptography, including mathematical background, classical ciphers, public key encryption, block and stream ciphers, cryptographic hash functions, digital signatures, common attacks, and basic security protocols. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD Course Prerequisites TBD

item.title: CIS 560 - Database System Concepts
item.description: Course Description Concepts, approaches, and techniques in database management. Representation of information as data, data storage techniques, foundations of logical data models, data retrieval, database design, transaction management, integrity and security. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Overview Not yet drafted — pending course-designer’s detailed pass. resources/reference/degree-maps/cs.md flags this “may become an elective,” and notes it as the elective-depth capstone on the computability arc seeded in CIS 115 and deepened in CIS 301 (P vs. NP, NP-completeness). It is also, as of the 2026-07-15 core-design regeneration, the only place in the degree map that still covers non-relational/NoSQL databases — that content was dropped from the required core as a confirmed, intentional scope reduction. See content/4-curriculum-design/threads/thread-data-structures.md for the full note.

item.title: CIS 561 - Introduction to Data Science in Practice
item.description: Course Description The development and implementation of computer science solutions to practical data science problems in science and industry. Implementing computer programs and applying computational tools to turn real-world data into knowledge and solve real-world data science problems. Includes a substantial capstone component. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD Course Prerequisites TBD

item.title: CIS 570 - Introduction to Formal Language Theory
item.description: Course Description Formal languages, automata, regular expressions, grammars, introduction to computability theory. Reading and writing informal mathematical proofs pertaining to these topics. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD Course Prerequisites TBD

item.title: CIS 575 - Introduction to Algorithm Analysis
item.description: Course Description An introduction to mathematical analysis of time- and space-complexity of algorithms, including worst-case, average-case, and amortized complexity. An examination of various algorithmic designs, such as greedy algorithms, divide-and-conquer algorithms, and dynamic programming algorithms. Techniques for proving correctness of algorithms. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Overview Not yet drafted — pending course-designer’s detailed pass. resources/reference/degree-maps/cs.md flags this “may become an elective,” and it’s the confirmed elective-depth home for P vs. NP (paired with CIS 560’s own elective-depth NP-completeness content) on top of the required CIS 300/301 algorithmic foundation.

item.title: CIS 580 - Fundamentals of Game Programming
item.description: Course Description Fundamental principles of programming games. Foundational game algorithms and data structures. Two-dimensional graphics and game world simulation. Development for multiple platforms. Utilization of game programming libraries. Design of multiple games incorporating topics covered. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD Course Prerequisites TBD

item.title: CIS 590 - Special Topics in Computer Science
item.description: Course Description Selected topics in computer science. Credit Hours 1–4 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD Course Prerequisites TBD

item.title: CIS 596 - Entrepreneurial Computer Science Project
item.description: Course Description Directed studies: selection, investigation and report on some topic not covered in prior courses; may include an implementation and/or experimentation component; may be done in collaboration with other students. Completion of a final report with literature review and project evaluation. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes Upon completion of this course, students will be able to: Analyze a complex computing problem and to apply principles of computing and other relevant disciplines to identify solutions. (ABET 1) Design, implement, and evaluate a computing-based solution to meet a given set of computing requirements in the context of the program’s discipline. (ABET 2) Communicate effectively in a variety of professional contexts. (ABET 3) Apply computer science theory and software development fundamentals to produce computing-based solutions. (ABET 6) Course Prerequisites TBD

item.title: CIS 598 - Computer Science Project
item.description: Course Description Directed studies: selection, investigation and report on some topic not covered in prior courses; may include an implementation and/or experimentation component; may be done in collaboration with other students. Completion of a plan, two reviews, and a final report with literature review and project evaluation. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Overview Not yet drafted — pending course-designer’s detailed pass. resources/reference/degree-maps/cs.md lists this as one of three choices (with CIS 643, DEN 591) for the Year 4 Capstone. This is distinct in purpose from CIS 400’s capstone-of-the-core: the Year 4 Capstone validates the whole degree plus specialization work, where CIS 400 validates the two-year core alone.

item.title: CIS 599 - Cybersecurity Project
item.description: Course Description Directed studies: selection, investigation and report on some topic not covered in prior security courses; may include an implementation and/or experimentation component; may be done in collaboration with other students. Completion of a final report with literature review and project evaluation. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD Course Prerequisites TBD

item.title: CIS 625 - Concurrent Software Systems
item.description: Course Description Architecture, design, modeling, implementation, and verification of concurrent, parallel, and distributed software; aspects such as real-time programming, parallel simulation; fault-tolerant programming; grid computing, embedded systems control. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Overview Not yet drafted — pending course-designer’s detailed pass. resources/reference/degree-maps/cs.md lists this as one of three choices (with CIS 520, CIS 525) for the Year 4 Systems Elective, and confirms it as legitimate elective depth sitting on top of CIS 300’s required concurrent-algorithms/thread-safe-data-structures content — the same “required foundation, elective depth” pattern used elsewhere (e.g., CIS 560/575 on top of CIS 300/301).

item.title: CIS 640 - Software Testing Techniques
item.description: Course Description Survey of software testing methodologies; evaluation of software testing strategies; experience in a variety of software testing practices. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD Course Prerequisites TBD

item.title: CIS 642 - Software Engineering Project I
item.description: Course Description The first semester of a two-semester capstone course. Current practices of software development, requirements, design, prototyping, measures and evaluation. Specification, design, and prototyping of a software system. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes Upon completion of this course, students will be able to: Analyze a complex computing problem and to apply principles of computing and other relevant disciplines to identify solutions. (ABET 1) Design, implement, and evaluate a computing-based solution to meet a given set of computing requirements in the context of the program’s discipline. (ABET 2) Communicate effectively in a variety of professional contexts. (ABET 3) Apply computer science theory and software development fundamentals to produce computing-based solutions. (ABET 6) Function effectively as a member or leader of a team engaged in software engineering activities. Course Prerequisites TBD

item.title: CIS 643 - Software Engineering Project II
item.description: Course Description Continuation of CIS 642. Final implementation, integration, and testing of a software system. Introduction to configuration management, project management, and software maintenance. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes Upon completion of this course, students will be able to: Analyze a complex computing problem and to apply principles of computing and other relevant disciplines to identify solutions. (ABET 1) Design, implement, and evaluate a computing-based solution to meet a given set of computing requirements in the context of the program’s discipline. (ABET 2) Communicate effectively in a variety of professional contexts. (ABET 3) Apply computer science theory and software development fundamentals to produce computing-based solutions. (ABET 6) Function effectively as a member or leader of a team engaged in software engineering activities. Course Prerequisites Prerequisite: CIS 642, which must be taken in the preceding semester (current catalog).

item.title: CIS 655 - Security and Reliability of Computing Systems
item.description: Course Description Fundamentals of security and reliability of computing systems from both hardware and software perspectives. Topics include symmetric and asymmetric cryptography, artificial intelligence (AI) safety and security, selected topics from hardware-based security, introduction to reliability and fault tolerance, hardware fault tolerance, and software fault tolerance. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD Course Prerequisites TBD

item.title: CIS 690 - Implementation Projects
item.description: Course Description The department will suggest various design or implementation projects for individuals or groups in areas such as translators, interpreters, microprogramming, minicomputer operating systems, graphics, numerical software, etc. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Goals and Learning Outcomes TBD Course Prerequisites TBD

item.title: MATH 200 - Logic and Sets
item.description: Course Description This course introduces the language and structures used for mathematical reasoning in computer science. Students translate statements into propositional logic, analyze truth and logical equivalence, work with normal forms and satisfiability, and use sets, functions, and relations to model discrete systems. Credit Hours 1 credit Course Goals and Learning Outcomes Measurable Outcomes. Through graded coursework, upon successful completion of this course, students will: Explain basic terminology and operations for sets, relations, and functions. Relate examples to the appropriate set, function, or relation model. Convert statements to propositional and predicate logic expressions. Course Prerequisites Prerequisite: College algebra

item.title: MATH 201 - Counting Finite Configurations
item.description: Course Description This course develops systematic methods for counting finite configurations. Students work with finite sets and cardinality, apply sum and product rules, use permutations and combinations, and solve problems with binomial coefficients, the Binomial Theorem, the pigeonhole principle, and inclusion-exclusion. Credit Hours 1 credit Course Goals and Learning Outcomes Measurable Outcomes. Through graded coursework, upon successful completion of this course, students will: Calculate the size of a finite set and distinguish between finite and infinite sets based on cardinality. Apply counting arguments such as the multiplication principle, inclusion-exclusion principle, and pigeonhole principle. Compute permutations and combinations of a set. Demonstrate knowledge of binomial coefficients and the Binomial Theorem. Course Prerequisites Prerequisite: MATH 200

item.title: MATH 202 - Recursive and Modular Computation
item.description: Course Description This course studies recursive processes and arithmetic on the integers. Students work with recursive definitions and recurrence relations, analyze arithmetic, geometric, and logistic sequences, use mathematical induction, and perform computations involving divisibility, prime factorization, modular arithmetic, greatest common divisors, and Euclid’s Algorithm. Credit Hours 1 credit Course Goals and Learning Outcomes Measurable Outcomes. Through graded coursework, upon successful completion of this course, students will: Apply proof techniques of direct proof, proof by contradiction, weak and strong induction. Distinguish between inductive and recursive definitions and formulas. Apply recursive definitions and solve basic recurrence relations. Perform computations involving modular arithmetic. Use Euclid’s Algorithm and compute the greatest common divisor of two integers. Course Prerequisites Prerequisite: MATH 201

item.title: MATH 203 - Graphs, Trees, and Networks
item.description: Course Description This course introduces graphs and trees as models for networks and discrete structures. Students use graph terminology, recognize important graph classes, work with matrix and weighted representations, apply traversal and shortest-path algorithms, and analyze trees, spanning trees, planar graphs, Euler paths, and Hamiltonian paths. Credit Hours 1 credit Course Goals and Learning Outcomes Measurable Outcomes. Through graded coursework, upon successful completion of this course, students will: Apply proof techniques of direct proof, proof by contradiction, weak and strong induction. Distinguish between inductive and recursive definitions and formulas. Apply recursive definitions and solve basic recurrence relations. Perform computations involving modular arithmetic. Use Euclid’s Algorithm and compute the greatest common divisor of two integers. Course Prerequisites Prerequisite: MATH 202

item.title: STATS 492 - Statistical Foundations of Data Science
item.description: This document describes a proposed computational statistics course to serve the common computing foundation being developed by the department of computing science. This course is intended to be housed in the Department of Statistics and will be co-designed with computer science faculty. Exact numbering is not yet determined. Also important to note is that between this course, the discrete mathematics sequence, and calculus, the following ABET accreditation requirements must be met: At least 9 semester credit hours (or equivalent) must include statistical inference and modeling, linear algebra, probability, data visualization, and optimization topics.
